idiom_name: struct state + Apply(ctx, Event) decider + database row + context deadlines
implementation_notes: Go ships no workflow runtime, so the manager is a small package: a row keyed by the correlation id holds the typed state, an Apply(ctx, Event) method switches on (state, event) to produce the next command, and a sweeper goroutine or scheduled job processes rows whose deadline has passed. context.WithTimeout bounds a single in-process await, but a deadline that must survive a restart belongs in the row as data, not in a context that dies with the process. Hand-rolling is right for short flows inside one service; once the flow must survive deployments and span services, a durable-execution SDK (Temporal Go SDK) provides the same pattern with managed history and timers.
pitfalls: State kept in a struct in memory (or a map guarded by a mutex) is lost on deploy; the row must be the only source of truth, and per-instance work must be serialised by a row lock or a keyed goroutine.
time.After inside a loop allocates a timer per iteration that only fires later; use time.NewTimer/Ticker and Stop it, or better, store deadlines and sweep them.
Redelivery after a restart is normal, so Apply must be idempotent per event id - otherwise the same reply advances the flow twice.
Goroutines started per message without a bound or a shutdown path leak when a step blocks, and a process manager that cannot be drained cannot be redeployed safely.
